hook.text: Two hundred rows, ten thousand columns of random numbers, and a label that's a coin flip. Cross-validated, this model scores eighty-five percent.

hook-why.text: Nothing in it can predict anything. Question six finds where the eighty-five came from.

hook-round.text: Language models didn't retire classical machine learning, and the first thing an ML round still tests is whether a model works on data it hasn't seen.

plan.text: Twelve questions. Ten are worked through: why models fail on new data, how to measure that honestly, and which number to report. Two are quick.

bias.text: Question one. Explain the bias-variance trade-off, and its decomposition.

bias-def.text: Bias is error from a model too simple for the pattern; variance, from fitting one training sample's quirks. With noise no model can remove, bias squared, variance and noise sum to the expected squared error on new data.

bias-sim.text: A simulation can measure all three. Draw five hundred training sets of fifty points from a known curve, and fit a tree to each.

bias-dart.text: At one point on the curve, the stumps' predictions bunch together, off target: that's bias. Trees six deep centre on the target, and scatter: that's variance.

bias-sum.text: Averaged along the curve, a stump's error is point two oh: point oh seven bias, point oh four variance, point oh nine noise. Depth three is lowest, at point one four, and deeper trees climb back up, almost all of it variance.

bias-data.text: The follow-up is what fixes each. Give the depth-six tree ten times the data, and its variance falls from point oh eight to point oh three. The stump's bias doesn't fall at all.

bias-real.text: On a real problem there's one dataset and no known curve, so you read the two from training and validation error.

fit.text: Question two. What is overfitting, and how do you combat it? It's a model that has memorized its training data: low training error, high validation error.

fit-curves.text: Learning curves show it. On a standard benchmark with ten inputs, five of them noise, an unpruned tree has zero training error at every size, and its validation error is still falling at two thousand rows.

fit-gap.text: The gap is variance, and a gap still closing says more data will help.

fit-fix.text: So get more data, cut capacity, regularize with L one, L two or dropout, augment the data, or stop early.

under.text: Question three. What is underfitting? Both errors high, and close together.

under-line.text: A straight line on the same data has two curves that meet within a few hundred rows, both near seven, and more rows won't move them.

under-fix.text: It needs more capacity, longer training, less regularization, or better features. Add a product of two inputs and a square, and its error falls from six point nine to four point six.

reg.text: Question four. L one versus L two regularization? Both add a penalty on the weights to the loss. They differ in what happens to a small weight.

reg-run.text: The page's run has twenty features, five of them informative. Ridge, the L two penalty, keeps all twenty: the useless ones shrink below a quarter, but none reaches zero. Lasso, the L one penalty, keeps exactly the five.

reg-why.text: L two pulls in proportion to the weight, so the pull fades as the weight shrinks. L one pulls just as hard all the way down, so a weight that isn't earning its keep lands on zero.

reg-prod.text: In production that's a saving: five features to compute at serving time, not twenty. With correlated features, lasso keeps one arbitrarily, and elastic net, which mixes both penalties, keeps the group.

measure-in.text: Every fix so far was judged on validation data. Next, how to keep that judgement honest.

split.text: Question five. Why split data into train, validation and test? Train fits the parameters, validation chooses between models and settings, and test is touched once, for an honest final estimate.

split-sim.text: Choosing is what makes a score optimistic. Make the labels coin flips, so every model is worth fifty percent. Try fifty settings, and keep the best on the forty validation rows.

split-result.text: Over two hundred repeats, the winner averages sixty-four percent on validation, and fifty on the test set.

split-prod.text: Tune on the test set, and you report sixty-four and ship fifty. And when the data has time in it, split by time: train on the past, and test on what came after.

leak.text: Question six. What is data leakage, and how do you prevent it? It's information the model won't have at prediction time getting into training, so offline scores rise, and production ones collapse.

leak-hook.text: Here's the eighty-five from the opening. Before cross-validating, it picked the twenty columns most related to the label using every row, including the ones each fold then held out.

leak-fold.text: Make that pick inside each fold, on its training rows, and it scores fifty-four, about what always guessing the commoner label gets.

leak-forms.text: The page's example, a scaler fitted on every row, changes nothing on its own data: eighty percent either way. What leaks hard is anything that saw the label.

leak-fix.text: So fit every transform inside the training split, as one pipeline, and audit features for proxies, like a refund flag in a fraud model, or a total computed with data from after the prediction.

cv.text: Question seven. What is k-fold cross-validation, and when do you use it? Split the data into k folds, train on all but one, validate on that one, and rotate until each fold has been held out once.

cv-run.text: The page's five folds score from seventy-five to eighty-seven and a half percent, and any one could have been your only validation set. Their mean, seventy-nine and a half, give or take four, is steadier.

cv-when.text: Use it when data is too scarce to set a validation set aside, or to compare models reliably. When a training run takes days, k folds cost k runs, and one hold-out wins.

cv-groups.text: The follow-up is what a fold must not split. Simulate sixty users, eight rows each, the label belonging to the user. Shuffled folds put every user on both sides, and a random forest scores ninety-seven percent by recognizing them. Grouped by user, it scores fifty.

cv-keep.text: So keep each user, session or patient inside one fold, and with time series, validate only forward.

score-in.text: Honest scores, then. Next, which score.

pr.text: Question eight. What are precision, recall, and F one score? Precision: of everything flagged, the share that was right. Recall: of everything that was there, the share you caught.

pr-page.text: F one is their harmonic mean, high only when both are. In the page's eight examples, three caught, one missed and one false alarm: all three come to point seven five.

pr-thresh.text: On a real model they trade off along the threshold. Simulate a fraud model on a hundred thousand transactions, one percent fraud. At a threshold of point five, precision is eighty-four percent and recall twenty-four. At point one, thirty-five and fifty-four.

pr-cost.text: Favor precision when false alarms are costly, recall when misses are: here, a false alarm blocks a good customer's card, and a miss loses the money. F one weighs them equally, which a business rarely does.

pr-capacity.text: Often capacity decides: if reviewers can check a thousand alerts a day, flag the top thousand. That catches four hundred and sixty-six of the nine hundred and ninety-five frauds.

auc.text: Question nine. What is ar-oh-see ay-you-see, and when does pee-ar ay-you-see matter more? The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate at every threshold. Its area is the chance that a random positive is scored above a random negative.

auc-fraud.text: The fraud model's area is point nine one, which sounds strong. But the false positive rate divides by ninety-nine thousand legitimate transactions. At one percent, that's a thousand false alarms, nearly twice the frauds caught.

auc-pr.text: The precision-recall curve never counts true negatives, so its area is what reviewers live with: point four six, against a chance level of point oh one, the fraud rate. When positives are rare, report pee-ar ay-you-see, and remember its baseline moves with the base rate.

imb.text: Question ten. What is class imbalance, and how do you handle it? When one class dominates, accuracy stops meaning anything: calling every transaction legitimate scores ninety-nine percent, and catches nothing.

imb-fix.text: Judge by precision, recall or pee-ar ay-you-see. Then weight the rare class in the loss, oversample it with SMOTE's synthetic rows or undersample the majority, move the threshold, or at the extreme, treat it as anomaly detection.
imb-fix.spoken: Judge by precision, recall or pee-ar ay-you-see. Then weight the rare class in the loss, oversample it with smote's synthetic rows or undersample the majority, move the threshold, or at the extreme, treat it as anomaly detection.

imb-trap.text: The follow-up is what reweighting does. With balanced class weights, recall at point five jumps from twenty-four percent to eighty-four. But the model now calls the average transaction twenty-two percent likely to be fraud, when one percent is, and its pee-ar ay-you-see falls from point four six to point three two.

imb-prod.text: So if anything downstream reads those as probabilities, recalibrate. That won't win back the ranking, so try lowering the plain model's threshold first. And resample only the training set: the test set keeps production's one percent.

r-early.text: Early stopping halts training once validation loss hasn't improved for a set number of epochs, the patience, and restores the best epoch's weights.

r-early-plateau.text: Set the patience too short, and it stops on a plateau: this small network, with a patience of twenty, stops at epoch sixty-eight, though its best is epoch one sixty-eight.

r-metrics.text: RMSE squares errors before averaging, so one big miss dominates it. MAE counts every unit of error alike, so one outlier moves it far less. Trained on squared error, a model predicts the mean; on absolute error, the median.

r-r2.text: R squared compares your squared error with always predicting the mean: one is perfect, zero is the mean's own score, and on new data it can go negative, which no share of variance explained could.

next.text: You can now tell whether a model will generalize. Next: the models themselves, and how they learn.
